text: And the young republic had a rough start.
It lost a border war with China in 1962 and fought Pakistan in 1965.
By the mid-60s, India was so short of food that it depended on grain shipments from
America.
Then came the Green Revolution.
New high-yield wheat and rice, irrigation and fertilizer.
Within about a decade, India could feed itself.
In 1971, India backed the independence struggle in East Pakistan and won a short war.
A new country was born, Bangladesh.
In 1975, Prime Minister Indira Gandhi declared an emergency.
Elections were suspended, opponents jailed, newspapers censored.
And when she finally called elections, the voters, the same voters of the picture symbols, threw her out.
For most of these years, India's economy was tightly controlled.
You needed government permission to make almost anything.
People called it the license raj.
In 1991, it all came to a head.
India nearly ran out of money.
Its foreign reserves could pay for only about three weeks of imports.
To get an emergency loan, the government did something unthinkable.
It flew 47 tons of its own gold to the Bank of England.
Remember Mahmoud's camels carrying India's gold away?
Remember Naoroji's drain?
Now India had to send its own gold to London.
Cargo?
47 tons of gold.
Destination?
London.
Keep it quiet.
Wait.
Didn't the British take enough already?
This time, we're getting it back.
And they did.
Because that crisis forced a revolution.
A quiet economist named Manmohan Singh, the new finance minister, stood up in Parliament
and quoted Victor Hugo, no power on earth can stop an idea whose time has come.
India opened up, lower taxes on imports, private companies welcome, foreign investment allowed.
Growth took off, and software companies in Bengaluru and Hyderabad began serving the
whole world.
In 2014, India reached Mars on its very first try for about $74 million, less than the Hollywood
space film Gravity cost to make.
In 2023, Chandrayaan-3 became the first spacecraft to land near the moon's south pole.
That same year, India became the most populous country on Earth.
Narendra Modi has been Prime Minister since 2014.
Today, India is the world's fifth largest economy, and the IMF expects it to pass Japan
next year.
To be fair, it still has a long way to go.
Hundreds of millions still earn very little, good jobs are scarce for the young, and critics
worry about pressure on the press and on religious minorities.
But the golden bird is climbing again.
So think about everyone who came to take something from this land.
Alexander, the Kushans, Mahmoud, Gori, Temur, Babur, Nadir Shah, a company from London.
Think about everything they carried off, gold on camels, a peacock throne, a diamond that
now sits in the Tower of London, and a drain of wealth that ran for 200 years.
And now, the question from the start.
Why did almost every robber end up staying?
Here's the answer.
India's wealth could always be carried away.
India itself never could.
The Kushans became champions of Indian Buddhism.
The Sultan's soldiers gave India ordo and kawali.
Babur arrived missing his melons and his great-great-grandson built the Taj Mahal.
Again and again, the invaders ended up eating India's food, speaking its languages, and
building its monuments.
Only one never moved in.
It ruled from an office in London, and it sent the money home.
By the time it left, India's share of the world had fallen to about four percent.
Remember that sailor at Calacan more than five hundred years ago?
So, he came for spices, and for cloth so fine that Europe named it after the port where
he stood.
Today, the world is coming back to buy from India again.
It's software, it's medicines, and yes, it's cloth.
India is once again one of the biggest cloth makers on Earth.
The golden bird lost its gold more times than anyone can count.
It never lost itself.
